column3: HTTP enables the use of intermediaries to satisfy requests through a chain of connections (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: HTTP enables the use of intermediaries to satisfy requests through a chain of connections.

column3: There are three common forms of HTTP intermediary: proxy, gateway, and tunnel (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: There are three common forms of HTTP "intermediary": proxy, gateway, and tunnel.

column3: A proxy is a message-forwarding agent that is chosen by the client, usually via local configuration rules (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: A "proxy" is a message-forwarding agent that is chosen by the client, usually via local configuration rules, to receive requests for some type(s) of absolute URI and attempt to satisfy those requests via translation through the HTTP interface.

column3: A gateway, also called a reverse proxy, is an intermediary that acts as an origin server for the outbound connection but translates received requests and forwards them inbound to another server or servers (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: A "gateway" (a.k.a. "reverse proxy") is an intermediary that acts as an origin server for the outbound connection but translates received requests and forwards them inbound to another server or servers.

column3: Gateways are often used to encapsulate legacy or untrusted information services, to improve server performance through accelerator caching, and to enable partitioning or load balancing of HTTP services across multiple machines (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: Gateways are often used to encapsulate legacy or untrusted information services, to improve server performance through "accelerator" caching, and to enable partitioning or load balancing of HTTP services across multiple machines.

column3: A tunnel acts as a blind relay between two connections without changing the messages (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: A "tunnel" acts as a blind relay between two connections without changing the messages.

column3: In HTTP, inbound means toward the origin server, whereas outbound means toward the user agent (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: inbound means "toward the origin server", whereas outbound means "toward the user agent".

column3: An interception proxy differs from an HTTP proxy because it is not chosen by the client (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: For example, an "interception proxy" [RFC3040] (also commonly known as a "transparent proxy" [RFC1919]) differs from an HTTP proxy because it is not chosen by the client.

column3: Proxies are often used to group an organization's HTTP requests through a common intermediary for the sake of security services, annotation services, or shared caching (`rfc9110#section-3.7`).
column5: Proxies are often used to group an organization's HTTP requests through a common intermediary for the sake of security services, annotation services, or shared caching.
